## Article: On the Computational Complexity of Quantum Error Correction
URL: https://jiilan.me/writing/quantum-error-correction-complexity
Date: 2025-03-18
Category: Physics · CS Theory

Quantum error correction remains one of the most technically demanding problems at the intersection of physics and computer science. The fundamental challenge is not merely physical — it is computational.

The threshold theorem guarantees that arbitrarily long quantum computations can be performed reliably, provided the error rate per gate is below a certain threshold. What is less discussed is the computational overhead this imposes and how it scales with the logical circuit depth.

Consider a surface code with distance d. The number of physical qubits required scales as O(d²), and the decoding problem — determining which errors occurred given the syndrome measurements — is itself a non-trivial computational task.

Minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) on the syndrome graph is the standard approach. But MWPM assumes an error model that may not reflect the actual noise characteristics of the hardware.

The decoder is not merely a classical post-processing step. It is an integral part of the quantum computation, and its complexity directly impacts the feasibility of fault-tolerant quantum computing.

If the decoding step cannot keep pace with the syndrome measurement rate, a backlog forms. This backlog grows the effective memory lifetime requirements, which in turn demands higher code distances, which further increases the decoding load.

Recent work on union-find decoders offers near-linear time complexity, but at the cost of suboptimal correction. The trade-off between decoder speed and correction quality is the central open question in practical quantum error correction.

## Article: Why Most Distributed Systems Papers Get Consistency Wrong
URL: https://jiilan.me/writing/distributed-systems-consistency
Date: 2025-02-04
Category: Systems Engineering

There is a persistent confusion in the distributed systems literature between consistency as a safety property and consistency as a liveness property. This confusion leads to systems that claim strong guarantees while silently violating them under partition.

Linearizability is the gold standard, but most papers that cite it do not actually implement it. What they implement is something weaker — often sequential consistency or even causal consistency — dressed up in linearizable language.

The distinction matters. A sequentially consistent system can return stale reads that a linearizable system cannot. In a financial system, this is the difference between a correct balance and an overdraft.

Most correctness proofs assume a synchronous or partially synchronous model. When the system enters an asynchronous period — which every real system does — the proof no longer applies.

A system that is correct "most of the time" is not correct. It is a system with undocumented failure modes.

What the field needs is not stronger consistency models, but more honest documentation of what guarantees actually hold and under what conditions they degrade.

## Article: The Geometry of Gradient Descent
URL: https://jiilan.me/writing/geometry-gradient-descent
Date: 2024-11-22
Category: Machine Learning · Mathematics

Gradient descent is typically presented as an optimization algorithm. This framing, while not wrong, misses the geometric structure that makes it work — and the geometric pathologies that make it fail.

The loss landscape of a neural network is a high-dimensional surface. Gradient descent traces a path on this surface, and the properties of the path depend on the curvature of the surface, not just the gradient.

The Hessian matrix at a point on the loss surface tells you everything about local curvature. Its eigenvalues determine whether you are in a valley, on a ridge, or at a saddle point.

In high dimensions, saddle points vastly outnumber local minima. Most points where the gradient is zero are saddle points, not minima.

The condition number — the ratio of the largest to smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian — determines how "elongated" the loss landscape is locally. A high condition number means SGD will oscillate, and the learning rate must be small enough to accommodate the steepest direction.

## Article: Notes on Compiler Correctness
URL: https://jiilan.me/writing/compiler-correctness-notes
Date: 2024-09-15
Category: Programming Languages

A compiler is a function from source programs to target programs. Correctness means this function preserves the observable behavior of the program. Stating this precisely is harder than it sounds.

Correct compilation means: for every source program P, the compiled program P' produces the same observable behavior as P when executed. Observable behavior includes outputs, side effects, and termination.

Not all invariants of the source program are preserved. Internal state, evaluation order, memory layout — these are implementation details that the compiler is free to change. The correctness criterion is about what the user can observe from outside.

CompCert remains the gold standard. It formalizes operational semantics for both C and the target assembly, and proves a simulation relation between them.

---

## Article: Information-Theoretic Limits of Lossless Compression
URL: https://jiilan.me/writing/information-theory-compression
Date: 2024-07-08
Category: Information Theory

Shannon's source coding theorem establishes the fundamental limit of lossless compression: no encoding can compress a source below its entropy rate. This is a clean, beautiful result. Its implications are less clean.

Entropy is a property of the source, not the data. A specific binary string does not have an entropy. The source that generated it does. Conflating these is the most common error in applied information theory.

Kolmogorov complexity asks: what is the length of the shortest program that produces this string? Unlike entropy, Kolmogorov complexity is a property of individual strings. Unlike entropy, it is also uncomputable.

In practice, compression algorithms do not compute entropy. They exploit specific structural patterns. The gap between a practical compressor and the entropy rate tells you how much structure the compressor is missing.

## Works

### Fault-Tolerant Distributed Compute Engine
Type: Systems · Infrastructure
A distributed computation framework designed around Byzantine fault tolerance. The system maintains consistency guarantees even under arbitrary node failures, using a novel consensus protocol optimized for compute-heavy workloads.

### Quantum Circuit Simulator
Type: Physics · Simulation
High-performance quantum circuit simulator that uses tensor network methods to simulate circuits beyond the reach of brute-force state vector simulation. Optimized for surface code circuits relevant to error correction research.

### Static Analysis Framework for Correctness Proofs
Type: Programming Languages
A framework for mechanized correctness proofs of compiler transformations. Built on top of a custom intermediate representation designed to make semantic preservation proofs tractable.

---

## Research Papers

### On the Computational Complexity of Real-Time Quantum Error Decoding
Published: Nature Quantum Information, 2025
Analysis of decoder complexity for surface codes under realistic noise models. Shows that standard MWPM decoders face a fundamental throughput bottleneck and proposes a hybrid approach combining fast approximate decoding with periodic exact correction passes.

### Consistency Envelopes: A Framework for Honest Distributed Systems Guarantees
Published: ACM SIGOPS, 2024
Introduces the concept of consistency envelopes — explicit specifications of the conditions under which a distributed system's consistency guarantees hold. Demonstrates that most production systems operate outside their documented guarantees during routine network events.

### Geometric Properties of Loss Landscapes in Over-Parameterized Networks
Published: ICML Workshop, 2024
Studies the Hessian spectrum of loss landscapes in over-parameterized networks, showing that the effective dimensionality of the optimization problem is much lower than the parameter count suggests. Proposes adaptive methods based on estimated curvature.
